candidates.source_body_excerpt: A Rochdale school that teaches children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) has been praised by Ofsted. Ofsted praised Redwood School for creating an environment where “there is no ceiling on what pupils can achieve”. This was highlighted in a glowing inspection of Redwood by the education regulator who also praised how leaders “place inclusion at the cornerstone of the school’s work” and how “pupils at all stages are ready and confident to learn”. Inspectors visited the special school, maintained by Rochdale Council, in September and under the new inspection framework, they found strong standards in 5 out of 7 areas. These areas were inclusion, attendance and behaviour, leadership and governance, personal development and wellbeing, and post-16 provision. The school also met expected standards in its achievement and curriculum and teaching. Ofsted also highlighted how the school’s careful adaptations to meet a diverse and complex range of needs enable pupils to make “meaningful progress from their individual starting points”. Inspectors also praised Redwood’s sixth form provision, which operates across three campuses in Rochdale, Heywood and Middleton and supports learners aged 16 to 19.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Wrexham u18's made it two wins on the spin thanks to a stoppage-time strike from Oliver McTweed in Saturday's 1-0 win at Preston North End. The young Reds host Rochdale u18's tomorrow looking to continue their impressive form, and Professional Development Phase Lead Coach Craig Knight was full of praise for his players after the game. Knight also emphasised the importance of late goals, insisting he believes they're a major part of Wrexham's success. Speaking to the club's media, he said: “We talked in pre-season about how many times we scored deep in stoppage-time last year. “It's a characteristic of our teams, but our football club as well, because it comes off the back of the first team scoring so many last-minute goals over the last three or four years. “We want that identity, that characteristic. "Ideally, you'd like to do it sooner, but if it takes 95 minutes, 99 minutes, whatever it is, then we'll do that.” Another positive from a successful afternoon for the academy was the return of Carrick Murphy from a long-term injury.

candidates.source_summary: A community initiative which offers free health checks across Rochdale, Heywood and Middleton, has found that 50% of people didn't know they needed medical attention.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A community initiative which offers free health checks across Rochdale, Heywood and Middleton, has found that 50% of people didn’t know they needed medical attention. Launched on October 31, 2025, the free Community Health Checks programme, commissioned by Rochdale Council and delivered by the Living Well Rochdale Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) team, has reached an impressive milestone, with 2,000 health checks carried out across the borough. The initiative aims to make essential health screening more accessible, particularly for residents who may face difficulties accessing traditional GP services or who might not otherwise seek a routine health check. The initiative has seen the Living Well Rochdale CVD team take its services directly into the community, with checks carried out at a range of locations, including community venues, GP practices, workplaces, places of worship and even local cash-and-carry stores. Each free health check includes blood pressure monitoring, height and weight measurements, and a simple finger-prick test to assess blood sugar and cholesterol levels. Residents also receive their Body Mass Index (BMI) and QRISK3 assessment, which helps estimate their risk of developing cardiovascular disease over the next ten years. These quick and convenient checks provide valuable information about an individual’s health, helping to identify potential concerns before they develop into more serious conditions. He joined back up with the Rochdale council delegation in Sahiwal – aimed at bringing closer ties between the two towns. “They didn’t know why they were holding me, “ Coun Ali added. “I went to the immigration desk and something came up on the computer. “We kept asking if I was under arrest and they said no. They didn’t seem to know why when we asked.” But when attempting to return home on October 28 from Lahore airport, the same thing happened again. This was when things really got scary for the Rochdalian.

candidates.source_summary: Cobblers forward Owen Dale says he is ‘really enjoying’ his time at the club and hopes the ‘floodgates now open’ after scoring his first goal against Rochdale on Saturday.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: The 28-year-old winger, who joined Town on a one-year deal at the end of the summer transfer window, produced another excellent performance and was on target with a well-taken finish after 11 minutes. “I’ve started to get into a bit of a rhythm now and I’m building those relationships with other players in the team,” said Dale. “My main aim is just to help the team get us to where we want to get to. “I’ve got to credit the boys, I can’t play the way I play without them and what they do behind me, and obviously I’m happy with the goal. “I’ve had a few where I’ve been a bit unlucky and I’ve been critical of myself because I feel I could have had four or five already. But now that first one has gone in hopefully it opens the floodgates.” On how he’s finding life at Sixfields in general, Dale added: “I’m really enjoying myself. The group’s top, as are the manager and the staff, and the way we play really suits me. It allows me to express myself and I’m enjoying being part of this team.” Dale’s goal was the least Cobblers deserved for a dominant first half display but a wobble after half-time put the result in doubt - until Elliott List and Lee Evans turned things around. “It was really important to get the win and obviously I’m happy on a personal note to get off the mark,” Dale continued. “It’s been a few games coming but hopefully I can kick-on and score a few more. “I thought we showed great resilience and the lads did a great job off the bench. We are disappointed with how we started the second half because that should have been a 3-0 game, not 3-2, after how we played in the first half. “We will look back at that and we’ll be critical of ourselves but these things happen and the resilience we showed is a credit to the group and to the manager and the staff and how we’re building. We’re getting better and better.”

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale have begun the search for Ian Watson’s successor after defeat at Northampton left Dale 22nd. Barnet visit Spotland on Saturday. Rochdale parted company with head coach Ian Watson on Sunday 22 November after a 3-2 defeat at Northampton Town left them 22nd in League Two. The club have begun the search for his successor ahead of Saturday’s home game against Barnet. In their statement on Sunday , Rochdale thanked Watson for his work at the Crown Oil Arena and said the recruitment process was already under way. He leaves five months after taking charge, with Dale two points clear of relegation and four wins from their opening 16 league games. Northampton and Rochdale began Saturday level on points. Two of the players he recalled to the starting line-up, Ed Francis and Cian Hayes, scored within two minutes of each other early in the second half to turn a 1-0 deficit into a 2-1 lead. It lasted just 12 minutes. Elliott List equalised before Lee Evans converted the penalty that settled the game, leaving Dale to travel home without a point despite having led with half an hour to play. “We didn’t start the game well at all,” Watson told the club’s post-match interview on Saturday. His departure was announced the following morning. Ian Watson succeeded Jimmy McNulty in June after McNulty guided Rochdale back into the Football League and left for Stockport. The former South Shields manager did take Dale into the second round of the FA Cup , beating Fleetwood 2-1 away earlier this month. Two League Two fixtures come before the home cup tie against Newport on 5 December. Barnet visit first, followed by a trip to Cheltenham on Tuesday 1 December.

candidates.source_summary: Chris Hogg revealed there was ‘a bit of angriness’ in the Cobblers dressing room despite their 3-2 victory over Rochdale on Saturday.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Northampton completely dominated the first half at Sixfields and had chances to be home and dry well before the break. They racked up 15 shots to Dale’s three and forced visiting goalkeeper Sam Waller into a string of saves. But they only had Owen Dale’s 11th-minute opener to show for their efforts and the away side scored twice in three minutes to turn the game around at the start of the second half, before Elliott List and Lee Evans rescued victory. "Even at the end, there was real relief in the dressing room in terms of the result but also there was a bit of angriness about not having the game out of sight before they got back into it,” admitted Hogg. "But sometimes you need these experiences in life and in football and you need to go through the hardships to go and better. You don't want it every week but it's the first time in a long time that the team has come back and won and that bodes really well for the future.” Asked why Rochdale were allowed to get back into the game, Hogg said: "If I had the answer to that it wouldn't have happened. I felt we created some really good chances in the first half, we had lots of shots and our attacking metrics were really good, and 1-0 was the very least we deserved. “It was just the quality of the finish that let us down and we spoke about that at half-time. The game should have been over, but we changed the shape in the second half and managed to wrestle back the momentum. The boys puffed their chests out and came out with three points.” Dale produced another excellent individual performance and was rewarded with his first goal for the club, drilling into the bottom corner after just 11 minutes. "I'm delighted for Owen,” Hogg added. “He's been terrific behind the scenes in terms of his work-rate and everything he does. He deserved that goal. “He's been chasing it a little bit, both in training and in games, but he's had a big impact on us and he's a great lad to work with and I was so pleased to see him get his goal.”

candidates.source_summary: Pennine Care NHS and Pennine Care Charity have teamed up with Rochdale AFC Community Trust to deliver a new football programme for girls aged six to 11 who are waiting for, or already receiving, support from Rochdale child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS).
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A pioneering football-based project is helping young girls in Rochdale build confidence, friendships and resilience through the power of sport. Pennine Care NHS and Pennine Care Charity have teamed up with Rochdale AFC Community Trust to deliver a new programme for girls aged six to 11 who are waiting for, or already receiving, support from Rochdale child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS). The free 36-week pilot uses fun football activities to help girls stay active and develop their confidence, social skills and emotional wellbeing in a safe and welcoming environment. The programme was developed following feedback from parents of children receiving support from CAMHS, who highlighted the need for activities to help their children build self-esteem and make friends. The project is funded by the Football Association’s Empower Her Fund, which supports opportunities for women and girls to get involved in football. Sessions are delivered by experienced staff from Rochdale AFC Community Trust. Sixteen girls have taken part so far, with early feedback showing how much they are enjoying the sessions and the opportunities to build confidence and make new friends. Anders Cox is clinical lead at Heywood, Middleton and Rochdale CAMHS, run by Pennine Care NHS Foundation Trust. Anders said: “Getting active, making friends and feeling part of something can all support young people’s mental health. This project gives the girls a fun and welcoming environment where they can build their confidence, learn new skills and enjoy being active together.”
candidates.source_title: New mental health football project kicks off in Rochdale

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A man who murdered his wife and hid her body under a bed for two days has been jailed for a minimum of 21 years and six months. Kyle Howard, 36, of Tweedale Street, was sentenced today at Manchester Crown Court. Police found the body of Keeley Aspinall, 44, known as Kiki, on May 25 at their flat on the Freehold Estate. Howard told police he had fatally stabbed Keeley two days earlier and was reporting the incident because her body was beginning to smell. When questioned, Howard said that the pair had been drinking and began to argue in the kitchen. Keeley was cooking at the time and had a knife in her hand as the pair began to “tussle”. Howard admitted he had his hands around Keeley’s neck and punched her, but he could not remember exactly how the knife ended up in Keeley’s chest, but he said it “just did”. A Home Office post-mortem exmination found that Keeley had suffered a stab wound to the chest, bruising to her neck consistent with strangulation and various other scratches and bruises on her body. Throughout the investigation, Greater Manchester Police’s Major Incident Team unravelled a pattern of domestic abuse from Howard toward Keeley.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: The sun appears to be setting on the famous Seven Sisters tower blocks in Rochdale . On Monday, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) announced their intention to demolish the goliaths that have dominated the town’s skyline since the 1960s . They want to replace the 766 flats, most of which sit empty, with 601 new homes. The scheme would provide a mix of flats and townhouses - with a shift towards more family homes from a setup of mainly bedsits and one-beds. The Seven Sisters - actually named College Bank - have become part of the furniture. Lots of Rochdalians having either lived there, or had friends and family live there. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter To imagine travelling down the M62 and not seeing the brutalist siblings protruding into the sky seems odd. But it only takes one trip around the estate to realise the blocks have gotten into a sorry state. The garages below are all boarded up, rubbish is littered outside and the tower blocks themselves are becoming tatty, with signs visibly falling apart. RBH, who own the land, say they are becoming more unsafe - which is why two blocks have already been closed and the rest are currently being emptied. The decision to rehouse all 229 flats left occupied was made in October 2025 . Only 78 households remain, but they’re due to be out by next summer. Of those still left, there is a strong contingent of campaigners hoping to stop the demolition. The Save the Seven Sisters group (ST7S) want to see the blocks refurbished instead and have even come up with a plan on how to do it, but RBH don’t agree it’s feasible. Tenants have lived in limbo for a decade - ever since RBH originally announced their intention to demolish 10 years ago. RBH has shifted its stance multiple times - moving from part-demolition, to ruling it out entirely in 2023, before putting ‘all options back on the table’ in 2024, then finally deciding to demolish them this week. It has been a turbulent time to say the least. It could be argued that the situation is no further on than 10 years ago, but the picture in Rochdale has dramatically changed since. Former Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham put together a taskforce in 2024 to look into alternatives to demolition. The taskforce is made up of Rochdale council , the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), the Rochdale MPs office, the Greater Manchester Tenants Union and RBH. The social housing provider says they have conducted surveys that suggest there are a number of structural issues with the blocks - which is the reason two of the blocks are currently out of action. In conjunction with the taskforce, RBH have costed up options for various forms of refurbishments and also demolition. Following a year-long review of those findings, the decision was finally made. RBH deemed it too expensive and believed it would take too long to refurbish the blocks, so opted to redevelop. They estimated that it would take 12 years to refurbish and cost £269m – around £388,000 per flat. Then, even after that, homes would have an expected lifespan of around 50 years, according to RBH. Following this, investigators also uncovered that Ali was not only dealing drugs at street level, but he was also managing other street dealers. candidates.source_summary: Janoi Donacien missed Saturday’s 3-2 win over Rochdale due his late return from international duty.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: The 33-year-old defender had been expected to feature at Sixfields having represented Saint Lucia in their Concacaf Nations League matches against Bermuda and Barbados. However, he was nowhere to be seen, and neither was fellow centre-back Max Dyche. Josh Powell was the only defender on an otherwise very attack-minded bench. “Janoi’s just recovering from all his travel,” explained Chris Hogg. “He’s had a lot of flights in the last seven days or so but he’s all good and hopefully we can freshen him up and give him the recovery he needs. “Max is all OK. I just wanted to go with an attacking bench today and I wanted those options and thankfully that’s what we needed in the end.” Hogg also confirmed that he does not have a designated penalty taker and it was Lee Evans’ call to grab the ball and assume responsibility from 12 yards when Cobblers won a late spot-kick during Saturday’s game. After Town pegged Rochdale back to 2-2 in a ding-dong tussle, referee Callum Jones pointed to the spot for handball, and Evans made no mistake, dispatching confidently into the bottom corner. Hogg said: “To be honest, the boys take penalties in training and we do different things, but I’m a big believer in feel in that moment on the pitch. Lee wanted to step up and there’s no doubt he’s got the technical quality. “He’s taken real leadership in a big moment for us and I’m delighted that he got that one because I thought he was a big part of the team in terms of the belief and the way he drove us forward and played forward and helped us get back into the game.”

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale have been left 22nd in the League Two table after a seven-game winless run. The dismal streak extended with a 3-2 loss against fellow strugglers Northampton Town on Saturday, putting head coach Ian Watson in real danger. And, on Sunday morning, it was confirmed that the Dale had parted ways with Watson, who was appointed as Jimmy McNulty ‘s replacement on a three-year deal in the summer. The search for Watson’s replacement has already begun. Here, we put forward three contenders who should be on Rochdale’s radar… Given his close connection with rivals Bury, Ryan Lowe may not be minded to take the vacant post at Spotland. However, Rochdale need EFL experience after poaching Watson from South Shields didn’t work out, and Lowe would bring that in abundance. His stint with Wigan Athletic was tough, but he did a steady job over the course of nearly three years at Preston North End and delivered League Two promotion in his time at Plymouth Argyle . He had them 4th in League One when he left for Deepdale too. Lowe’s EFL pedigree could be just what the Dale need to push away from the drop and further up the table in the long term. His locality ticks a box as well. Plenty of League Two clubs considering a change will have eyes on Andy Woodman . He was controversially let go by Bromley after only 10 League One games, despite leading them from the National League to the third tier in his five years in charge. Talk around a potential move to Crawley Town has been brought to an end by their appointment of Kevin Blackwell. Woodman is available for nothing and his pragmatic management focuses on simple but effective football, and he led a truly united squad at Bromley, helping them battle against the odds to reach League One.

candidates.source_summary: Northampton beat Rochdale 3-2 in a thrilling game at Sixfields.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
Northampton beat Rochdale 3-2 in a thrilling game at Sixfields.

Both teams had the lead at different stages of a topsy-turvy encounter but Lee Evans' 74th-minute penalty ensured the home side claimed all three points.

Rochdale goalkeeper Sam Waller denied Matty Warhurst early on before Northampton took a deserved lead on 11 minutes when Owen Dale latched onto James Maxwell's ball down the left wing, cut inside and drilled into the bottom corner.

Waller was a busy man throughout the first half as his reflexes denied Joe O'Brien-Whitmarsh before he also thwarted Dale and Joe Wormleighton.

Rochdale were second best up until the break but they were a different team in the second half and scored twice in as many minutes to turn things around.

Ed Francis' shot from 25 yards squirmed through Zach Jeacock before Cian Hayes slid home at the back post from Glenn Middleton's cross.

Northampton fought back impressively though, Elliott List tucking away Warhurst's cutback midway through the second half, before Evans won it from 12 yards with 16 minutes to go after a penalty was given for handball.

candidates.source_summary: Chris Hogg hails Northampton reaction against Rochdale Central Fife Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Northampton boss Chris Hogg hailed the “outstanding reaction” of his players after they fought back from 2-1 down to beat Rochdale 3-2. Owen Dale gave the Cobblers an early lead at Sixfields but two goals in as many minutes from Ed Francis and Cian Hayes turned things around at the start of the second half. However, Elliott List levelled just after the hour-mark before Lee Evans won it from the penalty spot with 16 minutes to play. “It was a bit of a roller-coaster and it’s another experience for us as a team and as a group of people,” said Hogg. “We’ve already been through a lot of experiences this season, some good and some not so good, but I’m really pleased for the players today – I thought their reaction in the second half was outstanding. “The game should have been dead and buried for me in the first half. One goal was the very least we deserved and I spoke at half-time about being ruthless and then you blink and you’re 2-1 down and that’s a lesson for us. “You can’t wait to go 2-1 down to start playing again, but Listy came on and I thought he was terrific. “We changed the shape slightly and we wrestled the momentum back.

candidates.source_summary: Rochdale manager Ian Watson described the penalty that proved decisive in Saturday’s 3-2 defeat at Sixfields as ‘really harsh’.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Kane Taylor was adjudged to have had his arm in an unnatural position when blocking Elliott List’s cross with 16 minutes to play. Referee Callum Jones took his time before pointing to the spot and Lee Evans made no mistake from 12 yards to complete Northampton’s comeback after Dale had found themselves 2-1 in front. Earlier, the home side dominated the first half and would have been out of sight if not for Sam Waller. The Rochdale goalkeeper made a series of saves both before and after Owen Dale’s opener. “We didn’t start the game well at all," admitted Watson. “The opposition got on top of us and deservedly took the lead. We came more into it later in the first half and did have a couple of chances before half-time. “We demanded more energy and more intensity in the second half and we got that and we scored the two goals, but I felt we then dropped off too much and gave them too much space. “But the penalty is really harsh. He’s falling back, the ball hits his hand from a very short distance and the ref takes a long time to think about it. It’s a tough one. “But there’s no papering over any cracks. We weren’t good enough to win the game and that’s because we didn’t start the game well enough. Our goalkeeper has made a couple of great saves and I felt we had a real fear and anxiety about getting on the ball and that’s not the team we want to be. “We wanted to change the mentality and mindset at half-time and come out on the front foot and the boys did really well to get back into the game. They did everything they could and they worked hard as hard as they could - that’s not the reason we didn’t win the game.”
candidates.source_title: Opposition view: Rochdale boss felt penalty call was ‘really harsh’

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Campaigners fighting to save Rochdale’s College Bank flats from demolition are calling on community leaders to step in and save the landmark tower blocks. Yesterday, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing announced that demolition and redevelopment of the site is the only viable option for the 61-year-old tower blocks known as the Seven Sisters. It said refurbishing them would cost at least £269 million and take up to 12 years — estimated at £388,000 for each of the 766 flats before VAT. RBH said the renovations would add another 50 years to the lifespan of the buildings, while redevelopment would provide 601 homes in a mix of sizes, creating a minimum additional 249 bedrooms, and the properties would last “significantly longer”. Reacting to the news, Greater Manchester Tenants Union said the decision was part of a “managed decline” overseen by the housing provider — a claim RBH denies. GMTU said: “Campaigners and the wider community are very disappointed with the decision to pursue demolition by RBH. “For 10 years the tenants and leaseholders of College Bank have suffered one mistaken decision after another. “RBH claims the decision is based upon ‘a detailed review of all available scenarios’ but it has only allowed for a costing of an overpriced refurbishment plan based upon installing a second staircase in each block of College Bank (under new regulations following the Grenfell disaster).”

candidates.source_summary: Andrew Kowalczyk had lived in a tower block in Rochdale for 27 years and now calls a bungalow home.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Andrew Kowalczyk lived on the College Bank estate for 27 years but says he is now happy in his new home After 27 years living in the Seven Sisters tower blocks in Rochdale, Andrew Kowalczyk did not want to leave. But he said he felt the demolition of the flats, which have dominated the town's skyline since the 1960s, was "inevitable" and he was now relieved to have been rehoused. Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) announced last week that the blocks would be bulldozed and replaced with a new College Bank estate of about 600 homes. It comes after a 10-year campaign by residents who wanted the flats to be refurbished and not knocked down but RBH said the demolition was the only "realistic" option. Kowalczyk, 61, who lived in the Mardyke block, said he was reluctant to move out of his "secure" home and the "great views" but he has since been rehomed in a bungalow in Lower Falinge and was now "delighted with it". Residents started to move out of the flats in October last year after long-term safety concerns were raised in October last year. The blocks are almost all empty, with 78 homes out of 766 currently occupied.

candidates.source_summary: A Grade II-listed former chapel in Middleton has been transformed into a new state-of-the-art engineering and manufacturing training facility.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A Grade II-listed former chapel in Middleton has been transformed into a new state-of-the-art engineering and manufacturing training facility. The new facility which opened this month has IT labs and an immersive virtual reality suite based at the landmark Reid building, part of Hopwood Hall College’s Middleton campus. As finishing touches are still being made to the exterior and landscaping, Cllr Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Council was given a preview this week, during a visit arranged to thank the college for its support of Rochdale Feel Good Festival. Hopwood Hall College was one of the main sponsors of this summer’s festival, an event it has supported since 2019, even hosting the main stage at the Rochdale campus in 2022 while the town hall closed for refurbishment. Julia Heap, principal and CEO of Hopwood Hall College, showed Cllr Smith around the site, including a stop at the historic chapel which has been transformed into an innovative skills hub with classrooms, computer labs and a virtual reality suite providing T-Level courses in engineering and manufacturing. Julia Heap, Hopwood Hall College principal and CEO (right) is thanked by Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council. Mrs Heap described it as possibly the most unique learning environment in the UK. She said: “This iconic building has always been a favourite with students, staff and college visitors, but now it has a completely new lease of life as a beacon for technical education and skills training while maintaining its character and heritage.
